permian-triassic-extinction.summary: The most severe extinction event known, eliminating roughly 80% of marine species and clearing the ground for the rise of the dinosaurs.

dinosaur-era.summary: Non-avian dinosaurs dominated terrestrial ecosystems for some 165 million years, from the Late Triassic until the end of the Cretaceous.
dinosaur-era.significance: Their 165-million-year run dwarfs our own. Anatomically modern humans have existed for roughly 0.2% as long, which is the proportion this timeline is built to make visible.
dinosaur-era.note: The earliest undisputed dinosaur fossils date to about 233 Ma; possible earlier forms push the origin back towards 243 Ma.

first-mammals.summary: Small, nocturnal and insect-eating, mammals spent 160 million years in the shadow of the dinosaurs before the asteroid gave them the daylight.

first-birds.summary: Feathered theropods took to the air. Birds are not the dinosaurs' relatives but their surviving branch, which means the group never actually went extinct.

flowering-plants.summary: Angiosperms coevolved with insect pollinators and came to dominate the land, eventually supplying almost everything humans eat.
flowering-plants.note: The bracket is the radiation, not the lineage. Angiosperms appear in the Early Cretaceous and hold most of the world's plant cover by the Late Cretaceous; they are of course still here, as are the eukaryotes, mammals and birds whose entries are bracketed the same way.
